item.title: curl Through Pivots: Internal API Discovery
item.content:encoded:
The interesting targets are never the ones facing the internet.

Series: curl — The Request Engine You Never Learned Properly Article: 14 of 16
Audience note: This article sits at the upper edge of the series. Articles 1–13 assumed. If you are still building confidence with bash loops and jq, finish Article 13 first and come back.
Scope note: Chisel, ligolo-ng, and SOCKS5 tunnel setup are out of scope. This article assumes an active SOCKS5 tunnel is already established and focuses entirely on how curl behaves inside one. If you are not yet comfortable setting up tunnels, TryHackMe’s “Wreath” network room covers this well.
Lab setup note: All output below comes from a self-built Docker pivot lab rather than a prebuilt CTF box — a foothold container (Alpine + sshd) reachable from the host, and an internal-api container (Flask + Swagger) placed on a Docker network marked internal: true, making it genuinely unreachable except through the foothold. This setup is cheap to reproduce (no VMs). The full lab — Dockerfiles, compose file, everything — is on GitHub: curl-pivot-lab. Clone it and docker compose up -d --build to follow along with every command in this article.

Getting a foothold on an external-facing machine is one thing. The more interesting targets are usually further inside the network — internal APIs, admin panels, management interfaces, and development environments that are unreachable from the internet.

A pivot extends your access. curl is how you use that access.

What Changes About HTTP Testing Through a Tunnel

When you are testing directly against a target, HTTP is straightforward. Through a tunnel:

DNS does not work the same way. Internal hostnames like api.internal or database.corp are only resolvable from inside the network. From your attacker machine, they do not resolve at all. You need to tell curl how to reach them.

Errors look different. A connection refused through a tunnel looks the same as an unreachable host. A timeout might mean the service is down, or it might mean the tunnel has dropped. Learn to distinguish these.

Speed is slower. Every request travels through the tunnel. Add latency to your --connect-timeout and --max-time values. What works in 5 seconds on a direct connection might need 15 seconds through a pivot.

The IP you appear as changes. Requests arrive at the internal target from the pivot machine’s internal IP — not from your external IP. Access controls that reference specific internal subnets now work in your favor.

Proving the boundary before you rely on it:

# From the attacker machine, direct to the foothold — works
ssh root@localhost -p 2222
# From the attacker machine, direct to the internal target — fails
curl http://localhost:5000
# curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost:5000 after 0 ms: Could not connect to server
# From inside the foothold itself, the internal target resolves and responds fine
curl http://internal-api:5000/health
# {"status":"ok"}

This confirms the setup actually models a real pivot scenario: the target is invisible from outside, reachable from inside.

SOCKS5 via Proxychains

Proxychains hooks curl’s network library and routes all connections through your configured SOCKS5 proxy.

# proxychains4.conf points to the SOCKS5 tunnel on 127.0.0.1:1080
proxychains curl http://internal-api:5000/health
[proxychains] config file found: /etc/proxychains.conf
[proxychains] preloading /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libproxychains.so.4
[proxychains] DLL init: proxychains-ng 4.17
[proxychains] Dynamic chain  ...  127.0.0.1:1080  ...  internal-api:5000  ...  OK
{"status":"ok"}

What works:

HTTP and HTTPS connections work reliably through proxychains. The requests go through the SOCKS5 tunnel to the pivot machine and from there to the internal target.

A correction on DNS behavior: older guidance on proxychains often warns that DNS resolution through it is inconsistent, and that you may need to resolve hostnames manually via /etc/hosts on the pivot. Testing against proxychains-ng 4.17 (the version Kali ships by default) did not reproduce this — hostname resolution through the tunnel worked cleanly:

proxychains curl -v http://internal-api:5000/health 2>&1 | grep -i resolv
# * Host internal-api:5000 was resolved.

If you hit DNS issues with proxychains, check which fork and version you’re running — proxychains-ng behaves differently from the older, unmaintained proxychains.

TLS certificate verification through proxychains:

proxychains curl -k https://internal.target.com

Expect to use -k in many pivot scenarios, but prefer --cacert if you have access to the internal CA certificate — it verifies the chain properly instead of skipping verification entirely. -k is the fallback when the CA isn't available to you, which in post-exploitation contexts is often the case — you are already inside the network, and the certificate's origin is rarely something you control.

Direct SOCKS5 with -x — The Cleaner Path

Curl has native SOCKS5 support. When possible, this is preferable to proxychains.

curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal-api:5000/health
{"status":"ok"}

The socks5h:// scheme (note the h) tells curl to pass hostnames to the proxy for resolution — the proxy resolves the hostname on your behalf, from inside the network. This solves the DNS problem that proxychains can have with older forks.

(Mnemonic: socks5h = "socks5 with hostname resolution" — the h reminds you that the proxy handles DNS.)

socks5:// (without the h) resolves hostnames locally before connecting through the proxy. Use socks5h:// for internal hostnames.

Setting up the tunnel this was run through:

ssh -D 1080 root@localhost -p 2222

-D 1080 turns the SSH session itself into a SOCKS5 proxy listening on local port 1080 — no separate tunneling tool required. By default this binds to 127.0.0.1 only, which is fine for single-machine use. If another machine on your network needs to route through the same tunnel, bind to all interfaces instead: ssh -D 0.0.0.0:1080 root@localhost -p 2222.

⚠️ Gotcha: on Alpine-based pivot boxes, ssh -D may connect fine but every tunneled request still fails with proxy closed connection. The usual cause is AllowTcpForwarding no sitting earlier in sshd_config than any line you've appended — sshd obeys the first match, not the last.
Fix it by editing the existing line in place instead of appending a new one: sed -i 's/AllowTcpForwarding no/AllowTcpForwarding yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Adding the full flag set for pivot work:

curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 \
  -k \
  --connect-timeout 15 \
  --max-time 30 \
  -s \
  http://internal.target.com/api/status

This is your baseline pivot curl command. -k for cert issues, longer timeouts for tunnel latency, silent mode for clean output.

Auth Token Forwarding Through a Pivot

When you compromise a machine, look for authentication credentials that can be reused against internal services.

Likely locations:

# Configuration files
find /opt /var/www /home -name "*.conf" -o -name "*.env" -o -name "*.config" 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l "token\|api_key\|password\|secret" 2>/dev/null
# Environment variables
env | grep -iE "token|key|secret|password"
# Shell history
cat ~/.bash_history | grep -iE "curl|token|auth|bearer"
# Application directories
cat /var/www/html/.env 2>/dev/null
cat /opt/app/config.yml 2>/dev/null

On the lab’s foothold machine, a token was planted exactly where this kind of sweep would find it:

cat /opt/app/.env
# INTERNAL_TOKEN=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.fake.payload

First, confirm the target endpoint is actually gated — request it with no credentials:

curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal-api:5000/api/v1/admin/users
# {"error":"unauthorized"}

Now inject the found token:

INTERNAL_TOKEN="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.fake.payload"
curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INTERNAL_TOKEN" \
  http://internal-api:5000/api/v1/admin/users
{"users":["admin","jdoe","svc-backup"]}

Internal APIs are frequently accessed via service-to-service tokens with broader permissions than user tokens. A token found in a configuration file may have admin access to internal systems — exactly what happened here: a token sitting in a .env file unlocked an admin-only user listing on a host that was unreachable five minutes earlier.

Internal API Endpoint Discovery Patterns

External APIs are often documented. Internal APIs rarely are. Enumerate common paths:

TARGET="http://internal-api:5000"
PROXY="socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080"
for route in \
  /health \
  /api/v1/admin/users \
  / \
  /apispec_1.json \
  /openapi.json \
  /swagger.json \
  /api-docs \
  /v2/api-docs \
  /swagger \
  /api; do
    CODE=$(curl -x $PROXY -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 10 "$TARGET$route")
    echo "$CODE $route"
done
200 /health
401 /api/v1/admin/users
200 /
200 /apispec_1.json
404 /openapi.json
404 /swagger.json
404 /api-docs
404 /v2/api-docs
404 /swagger
404 /api

/apispec_1.json is Flasgger-specific (the library this lab's API uses). It's worth running the broader list above regardless of framework — /openapi.json and /swagger.json are common defaults, /api-docs shows up on a few Node/Express setups, and /v2/api-docs is Spring Boot's convention. Which one hits depends entirely on what's serving the app.

⚠️ Gotcha: avoid naming the loop variable path if you're on zsh. It's a reserved variable tied to $PATH, and reassigning it will quietly break your shell's command lookup for the rest of the session. Use route or any other name instead.

Read the 401s, not just the 200s. A 404 means nothing is there. A 401 means something is there and it’s guarded — that’s a target worth coming back to with credentials, not a dead end. In the sweep above, /api/v1/admin/users returning 401 was the signal to go hunt for a token.

Swagger / OpenAPI: The Internal API Attack Surface Nobody Hardens

When /swagger, /swagger-ui.html, or /openapi.json returns a 200, you have found something significant.

Swagger UI is a developer tool that generates an interactive web interface from an OpenAPI specification. It documents every endpoint, every parameter, every expected request format. It was designed for development environments and is frequently left running in production internal deployments because “no one outside can reach it anyway.”

That reasoning stops being true the moment there is a pivot.

# Download the OpenAPI spec
curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 -s \
  http://internal-api:5000/apispec_1.json | python3 -m json.tool
{
    "definitions": {},
    "info": {
        "description": "powered by Flasgger",
        "termsOfService": "/tos",
        "title": "Internal Corp API",
        "version": "0.0.1"
    },
    "paths": {
        "/api/v1/admin/users": {
            "get": {
                "responses": {
                    "200": {
                        "description": "list of users"
                    },
                    "401": {
                        "description": "unauthorized"
                    }
                },
                "summary": "Admin users endpoint"
            }
        }
    },
    "swagger": "2.0"
}

Reading the spec gives you:

  • All available endpoints and their methods
  • Required parameters and their types
  • Authentication schemes (Bearer, Basic, API key)
  • Schemas for request and response bodies
  • Example values

This is the complete API attack surface documented for you. In this case, the spec confirmed /api/v1/admin/users exists, takes GET requests, and returns either a 200 or a 401 — turning a guess from the earlier discovery sweep into a documented fact before a single credential was tried. Work through the endpoints systematically using the curl patterns from earlier articles.

Internal VHost Discovery Through a Pivot

Internal servers often host multiple virtual hosts accessible by hostname. From outside the network, these hostnames do not resolve. From your pivot position, you can probe them.

Enumerate common internal naming patterns:

PROXY="socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080"
for hostname in \
  admin.internal \
  dev.internal \
  api.internal \
  db.internal \
  jenkins.internal; do
    CODE=$(curl -x $PROXY -s \
      -H "Host: $hostname" \
      -o /dev/null \
      -w "%{http_code}" \
      --max-time 10 \
      "http://internal-api:5000/")
    echo "$CODE $hostname"
done
200 admin.internal
200 dev.internal
200 api.internal
200 db.internal
200 jenkins.internal

Reading a flat result correctly: every hostname above returned the same 200. On a single-app target with no vhost routing configured, that is the expected (if unglamorous) result — it tells you this particular server is not splitting traffic by hostname. The technique only pays off against a real multi-tenant server, where different hostnames return different status codes or response sizes. A hostname that returns a different status code or different response size than the default vhost has active content worth following up on.

Tip: when every hostname returns the same status code, don’t stop there — compare response sizes instead. Add -w "%{size_download}" to the loop. Two hostnames both returning 200 can still be serving completely different content, and a size difference is often the only sign of that.

Structuring Output During a Timed Pivot Window

Pivot access in real engagements is often time-limited — the tunnel may be detected, the session may expire, or the engagement window is finite. Capture everything you find immediately.

TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
PIVOT_DIR="pivot_output/$TIMESTAMP"
mkdir -p $PIVOT_DIR
PROXY="socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080"
TARGET="http://internal-api:5000"
for route in /health /api/v1/admin/users /apispec_1.json; do
  curl -x $PROXY -s --max-time 10 \
    "$TARGET$route" \
    -o "$PIVOT_DIR/$(echo $route | sed 's|^/||; s|/|_|g').txt" \
    -w "%{http_code} $route\n"
done
echo "Output saved to: $PIVOT_DIR"
ls -la $PIVOT_DIR
200 /health
401 /api/v1/admin/users
200 /apispec_1.json
Output saved to: pivot_output/20261112_225629
total 20
drwxrwxr-x 2 kali kali 4096 Nov 12 22:56 .
drwxrwxr-x 3 kali kali 4096 Nov 12 22:56 ..
-rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali  314 Nov 12 22:56 apispec_1.json.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali   25 Nov 12 22:56 api_v1_admin_users.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali   16 Nov 12 22:56 health.txt

(The sed swap above drops the leading slash before converting the rest to underscores — api_v1_admin_users.txt reads a lot cleaner than _api_v1_admin_users.txt.)

Naming convention:

YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS/ — timestamp at the top of the directory means all output from a pivot session is grouped. If you run multiple pivot sessions, the directory structure keeps them separate. Never dump files into the working directory without a timestamp — you will lose track of which session found what.

The techniques in this article turn a foothold into access across the internal network. curl’s native SOCKS5 support, combined with the authentication, enumeration, and pipeline skills from earlier articles, gives you a complete internal recon workflow from the command line.

item.title: Performance Testing in Production on Kubernetes: A Practical Guide
item.content:encoded:
Validating staging results safely, without touching real users.

Performance testing in production on Kubernetes. The same load test runs in a staging cluster and a production cluster side by side, while real users are never touched.

In the previous article, I turned staging benchmarks into a capacity plan for Traefik, the ingress controller replacing NGINX on our platform. Every number in that plan came from a staging cluster.

Production isn’t staging. It’s a bigger cluster, with other workloads on the same nodes and far more network rules. So before moving any real traffic, I had one question: do the staging results hold in production, and can I find out without putting real users at risk?

They didn’t hold. Production delivered less than half of staging’s throughput. Finding out why taught me more than the benchmark itself, and my first explanation turned out to be wrong.

Here’s how I tested production safely, what the gap turned out to be, and how I decided whether it mattered.

Start With a Test That Can’t Hurt Anyone

The timing made a production test possible. Traefik was already deployed in production, but it wasn’t serving customers yet. Every real request still went through NGINX. That meant Traefik could be loaded hard without any user noticing, as long as the test stayed completely off the customer path.

Each safety measure had a specific job:

  • A separate path. k6, an open-source load-testing tool, ran inside the cluster and sent traffic straight to the Traefik pods. There was no DNS or firewall change, so real users kept going through NGINX.
  • A unique test hostname. No real user uses it, so the test route couldn’t collide with a real one.
  • A test certificate. The test route used a self-signed certificate, so it never requested a real one or used up certificate-authority rate limits.
  • A throwaway backend. A static page served the test traffic. I checked it on its own first, far above the test’s load, so it couldn’t become the limit.
  • A narrow network rule. Only the k6 pods were allowed to reach Traefik on the test path.
  • One label on everything. Every test resource carried the same label, so a single command deleted them all, and a second command confirmed nothing was left.
  • A quiet window. Traefik was idle, but it shared nodes with real workloads, so I ran the test at a low-traffic time and watched node CPU and memory throughout.

One more step protects the conclusion rather than the users: run the test in staging first. Before touching production, I ran it in staging again. It reproduced about 9,000 requests per second on 2 pods with 2 cores, close to the 8,400 measured in the last article. That proved the test itself was trustworthy, so any difference in production would belong to production.

Run the Same Test in Both Places

A comparison is only fair if everything else matches. Both clusters ran:

  • Traefik: the same version, the same Ingress rules, 2 pods with the autoscaler pinned, and a 2-core CPU limit per pod
  • Backend: the same static page, sized so it was never the limit
  • Load: the same k6 sweep from 4 to 1,600 concurrent users, a 30-second warm-up at each level, keepalive on, and three trials per level reported as the median

The only configuration difference was memory. Production pods had a larger memory limit, and memory never came close to being the issue.

I also set the pass mark before running anything. Results between test sessions already moved by 20 to 30% in staging, so production passed if it landed within that range of staging.

It didn’t pass. Production peaked at about 3,800 requests per second, 42% of staging’s 9,000. p95 latency at the peak, the response time that 95% of requests beat, rose from about 14 ms to 36 ms. Both clusters had zero errors at every level, and the curves had the same shape. Production simply topped out lower.

A gap that size is easy to panic over. Before chasing the cause, I checked what it meant.

Check the Gap Against What Matters

Even at 42% of staging, production’s peak was still more than 40 times our real peak traffic. It wasn’t a capacity risk, and it didn’t block the migration.

That didn’t make it safe to ignore. An unexplained gap is a risk in itself. It could be something that gets worse as traffic grows, or something that also slows down other services on the same nodes. And if the cause was Traefik, the capacity plan from the last article would be wrong.

So the migration kept moving, and the investigation started in parallel.

Find the Cause One Layer at a Time

First, I ruled out the obvious suspects. Each one was either identical in both clusters or had plenty of room:

  • Node CPU: production nodes were 13 to 42% busy, with most cores idle
  • Node memory: no out-of-memory kills and no evictions
  • Hardware and operating system: the same machine type, image and kernel
  • Backend: far above the test’s load
  • Traefik configuration: identical in both clusters

Then I made my first guess. At the peak, each production CPU core handled about a third of the work of a staging core, about 1,030 requests per second against 3,140. Production Traefik was also using 92% of its CPU limit, against 72% in staging. It looked like the production hosts had slower CPUs.

It was a reasonable guess, and it was wrong. The problem was the evidence. Throughput depends on the network as well as the CPU, so a throughput test can show that something is slow, but not where.

So I changed one layer at a time, and added the test that was missing: one that uses the CPU and nothing else.

  • CPU and memory benchmark on the node, no network at all: 11.3 seconds in production against 10.3 in staging. CPU steal, the time a virtual machine loses to other machines on the same host, was 0% in both, and the clock speed was the same.
  • Backend alone, plain HTTP, Traefik bypassed: 18,400 requests per second in production against 40,200 in staging, 2.2× slower with neither TLS nor Traefik involved.
  • Time per network call: 1.47 ms in production against 0.66 ms in staging, 2.2× slower again.
  • Network policies in the cluster: about 17,300 in production against 12,000 in staging, so production’s network rule set was 45% bigger.

The CPU was fine. Everything that crossed the network was about twice as slow, even without Traefik.

The best explanation is the cost each connection pays to cross the cluster’s network layer. On these clusters, that layer is Cilium, the network plugin, which applies network policies and tracks connections using eBPF, small programs that run inside the Linux kernel. Traffic to a Kubernetes Service address also goes through kube-proxy, which turns that address into a pod address using routing rules. Both do more work per connection in a bigger cluster, with more policies, more workloads and more connections to track.

That’s our best explanation, not a proven one. The test couldn’t separate kube-proxy’s share from Cilium’s. A follow-up that sends traffic once to a pod address and once to a Service address would split them.

When a result looks like a CPU problem, add a test that uses the CPU and nothing else. That one test turned “slow hosts” into “slow network path” and pointed any future fix in the right direction. Faster CPUs wouldn’t have helped.

If the cost sits in the platform’s network path, it doesn’t belong to Traefik. It should hit any controller on that path. That was the last thing to check.

Compare Against What You Run Today

Comparing production Traefik with staging Traefik answers “is production slower?” It doesn’t answer the question that matters for a migration: will users notice the switch? For that, the fair comparison is Traefik against the NGINX serving customers today, in the same cluster, on the same path.

I ran both back to back, through each controller’s own Service, with the same domain, the same HTTPS requests and the same steady rate, set above our real peak traffic. Each run lasted three minutes after a short warm-up.

Where almost every request lands, the two were effectively the same. The median was 29.6 ms for Traefik and 29.3 ms for NGINX, and p95 was within 8 ms. Neither returned a single error, and Traefik used less CPU per pod than NGINX at this load.

Traefik’s p99 was the one clear difference: 328 ms against 91 ms. It’s still well under a second, and it’s worth watching after the switch. At the very tail, both controllers hit the same worst case of about 2 seconds. A worst case that matches across two different controllers points to the shared network path again, not to either controller.

So Traefik was slower in production than in staging, but so was the platform under it. Against the NGINX already serving users, it was on par for almost every request.

What It Means for the Capacity Plan

Three conclusions came out of this:

  • Staging’s absolute numbers don’t transfer. Production’s peak was 42% of staging’s, so any plan built on staging’s raw throughput would overestimate production by more than double.
  • Ratios against the current controller are safer. The plan from the last article compared Traefik with NGINX, and both run on the same network path in production. A slower network path should slow both controllers alike, so the ratio is the safer number to plan with. Production’s lower peak still left more than 40 times our real peak traffic.
  • Fix the right layer. If more capacity is ever needed, the work belongs in the network path, such as kube-proxy and Cilium settings. Bigger CPUs wouldn’t move the number.

With those three in hand, the performance question was settled, and the migration could move on to the next risk.

Checklist

Before you trust a production performance test, check each of these. Each one either protects your users or protects your conclusion.

  • Keep the test off the customer path. Use a separate route, a unique hostname, a test certificate and a narrow network rule, with no DNS or firewall change.
  • Prove your test in staging first. If it reproduces staging’s earlier numbers, any difference in production belongs to production.
  • Set the pass mark before you run. Base it on the run-to-run variation you already know, so the result can’t move the goalposts.
  • Judge the gap against real traffic. A large gap with plenty of headroom is an investigation, not an emergency.
  • Change one layer at a time. Include a test with no network at all, because throughput alone can’t tell you where the time goes.
  • Compare against what you run today. The fair question for a migration is whether the new system is worse than the old one, on the same path.
  • Clean up with one command. Label every test resource, delete them together, and confirm nothing is left behind.

Together, they let you test production hard without asking your users to take the risk.

Final Thoughts

I expected the production test to be a formality. Staging had already answered the capacity question. Production disagreed by more than half, and my first explanation for it was wrong.

The test that settled it wasn’t a bigger load test. It was a small one that left the network out. And the comparison that mattered wasn’t staging against production. It was the new controller against the old one, on the same path.

So don’t assume staging tells the whole story. Staging tells you how your software behaves. Production tells you how your platform behaves. Test there safely, and compare against what you already run.
